In a video Monday outlining his plans for his first 100 days in office, Trump said he will "direct the Department of Labor to investigate all abuses of visa programs that undercut the American worker." Trump wasn't specific about what he would do if any abuses were found. But if he is looking to satisfy many supporters of his populist policies, he could start by making changes to the H-1B visa, the guest worker program that draws the most criticism. Under the H-1B program, 85,000 workers and graduate students enter the U.S. each year, a limit set by U.S. law. The visas can last up to six years. Sometimes the guest workers go on to get green cards. The goal of the program is to bring in specialized, highly skilled employees who aren't available in the U.S. But the problem is that many employers use the visa simply to hire workers with ordinary skills at a lower wage, explains Ron Hira, associate professor of public policy at Howard University. "I'd say that more than half the visas are used to help facilitate the offshoring of U.S. jobs," said Hira, an expert on immigration and outsourcing. "And certainly more than half is used for cheaper labor — probably closer to 65 percent." Just as concerning to Hira is that guest worker visas are tied to their employers, creating a sort of de facto indentured servitude that allows employers the ability to exploit foreign employees. texts.full_text: a day into to-do lists), it pains me to say it, but the no-planners may have a point. I've found that having a backup plan can sometimes serve as a psychological crutch, allowing us to coast through life without truly committing to our goals. It's like having a parachute while learning to skydive; sure, it's safer, but it also robs you of the thrill and the necessity of learning to fly. Think about it: when you have a backup plan, you're not fully invested in the primary plan. You're hedging your bets, which can lead to half-hearted efforts and a lack of commitment. It's the equivalent of having a safety net while trying to learn a new trick—you might not put in the same level of focus and determination because, hey, if you fall, you'll be fine. Moreover, a backup plan can become a distraction. It's like having a spare key to a house you're trying to break into—you're so focused on the possibility of the spare key that you're not giving the lock your full attention. The backup plan can become a mental crutch, a safety blanket that we cling to, preventing us from fully embracing the uncertainty and challenge of the primary plan. But here's the catch: not having a backup plan doesn't mean you should be reckless. It means you should be fully committed to your primary plan. It means you should be willing to take risks, to fail, and to learn from those failures. It means you should be willing to embrace the uncertainty and the challenge, to put in the hard work and the determination, and to truly commit to your goals.
